cards.hook: Under skew, Black-Scholes delta over-hedges your index option.
cards.body: Black-Scholes delta assumes volatility stays put when spot moves. In equity index markets it doesn't: spot falls, implied vol rises, and your option reprices on both. The true hedge ratio is delta plus vega times the expected vol change per unit of spot. For index options that second term is negative, so the **minimum-variance delta is smaller than the Black-Scholes delta**. Hull and White reported this empirically for S&P options. Hedge with the textbook number and you carry more hedge than the risk needs. The excess shows up as P&L noise that you will be tempted to blame on gamma.
cards.depth: The size of the correction depends on whether the surface behaves sticky-strike or sticky-delta, which is a regime question. In markets with inverse skew, such as some commodities, vol tends to rise with spot and the adjustment flips sign.

cards.hook: Training was fair use; the pirated library was the liability.
cards.body: In Bartz v. Anthropic, Judge Alsup held in June 2025 that training on purchased books was **fair use, but building a permanent library from pirate sites was not**. That split is what practitioners keep flattening into 'AI training is legal.' The case then settled for a reported $1.5 billion, roughly $3,000 per work across about 500,000 books. The exposure was driven by how the data was acquired, not by what the model learned from it. Diligence on a training set is now a provenance question first and a transformation question second.
cards.depth: Kadrey v. Meta, decided days later by Judge Chhabria, also favored the defendant, but on a thin record. He signaled that market dilution of the authors' works could defeat fair use with better evidence. Neither ruling binds the other.

cards.hook: Average your forecasters, then push the average toward the extremes.
cards.body: Each forecaster holds a different slice of the evidence. A plain average blends their probabilities toward the middle, as if everyone had the same weak information. If their errors are partly independent, the pooled evidence is stronger than any single view, so the **simple mean is systematically underconfident**. Extremizing means pushing the aggregate away from 50% by a tuned factor. The Good Judgment Project found this improved accuracy over the raw mean in its tournament data. The more diverse and independent the forecasters, the more extremizing helps.
cards.depth: The caveat is correlated sources. If everyone read the same headline, there is no independent information to compound, and extremizing just amplifies a shared error. Tune the factor out of sample, never in sample.

cards.hook: Write the if-then trigger; it offloads initiation from willpower to cue.
cards.body: Task initiation is where the activation threshold bites. 'I will start the brief today' leaves the start to in-the-moment effort. An implementation intention fixes the trigger in advance: **'If I close the laptop at lunch, then I open the brief and write one line.'** The cue, not a decision, launches the behavior. Gollwitzer and Sheeran's meta-analysis reported a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment. Gawrilow and Gollwitzer also reported benefits for children with ADHD on tasks that depend on inhibition. The trigger must be a concrete event you already hit, and the action must be tiny.
cards.depth: Write the plan once, somewhere you will see it at the cue. Stack no more than two or three. Vague triggers like 'when I have time' fail because nothing in the environment fires them.

cards.hook: Niederhoffer's 1997 wipeout came from selling puts the past called safe.
cards.body: On Monday, October 27, 1997, the S&P 500 fell roughly 7% on the Asian crisis, and trading was halted by circuit breakers. Victor Niederhoffer had sold large amounts of deep out-of-the-money S&P puts, which looked like free premium across his sample history. His funds were reported wiped out as the margin calls hit. The market rebounded the next day. That rebound was worth nothing to him, because **margin calls end the game before mean reversion pays**. His strikes were reasonable against the data he had. The loss came from the leverage behind them.
cards.depth: Lesson for sizing: a short-tail position has to survive a move larger than anything in your sample, and survive it before the recovery. The sample's worst day is a floor on the risk, not a ceiling.

cards.hook: Recall it: why does doubling order size not double impact cost?
cards.body: Think of the square-root law before you read on. Impact scales with volatility times the square root of size over daily volume. So doubling your size multiplies cost by the square root of two, about 1.41, an increase of roughly 41 percent. Cost per share rises more slowly than size, but total cost still grows, and your edge per share does not. Eventually marginal impact meets marginal alpha. That point is your **capacity ceiling**, and a fixed one-lot backtest never shows it.
cards.depth: Before trusting a Sharpe, ask what size it was earned at. Rerun the backtest with fills penalized by a square-root impact term at two, five and ten times your size. The size where the net edge hits zero is the real capacity of the strategy.

cards.hook: Your calendar spread trades forward variance, not just theta.
cards.body: Selling the front month and buying the back at the same strike looks like a theta harvest. The cleaner view: total variance is additive in time, so the market implies a **forward variance** between the two expiries, equal to (back vol squared times back time, minus front vol squared times front time) divided by the time gap. You are long that forward window and short the near one. If front IV is bid for an event, the forward vol embedded in your spread is low, and the trade is cheap. If the term structure is inverted, you are paying for a window the market already fears.
cards.depth: Practical check: compute the forward vol before entering. Compare it to your estimate of realized vol for that window, not to either leg's quoted IV. After an event, the front leg's IV collapses far more than the back's, which is why earnings calendars are really forward-vol trades.

cards.hook: Imagine the deal already failed; you will find more reasons.
cards.body: Gary Klein's pre-mortem rests on a 1989 study by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington. Subjects who imagined an event had already happened generated reasons for it with roughly 30 percent more accuracy and detail than those asked what might happen. The mechanism is **prospective hindsight**: certainty about the outcome shifts the brain from judging plausibility to explaining a fact. The group also loses the social cost of being the doubter, because failure is assumed, not predicted. Run it before signing, not after the post-mortem.
cards.depth: Write the failure in the past tense, privately and silently, for two minutes before any discussion. Pooling the lists afterward avoids the anchoring that a first speaker creates. Then rank causes by how cheaply you could still prevent them.

cards.hook: Delay discounting means a deadline next week doesn't exist yet.
cards.body: Reward value falls hyperbolically with delay, and meta-analyses find that the curve is steeper in ADHD. A deadline seven days out is heavily discounted, so it exerts almost no pull today, while the cost of starting is immediate. The move is not more willpower. **Shorten the delay**: convert the distant deadline into a chain of near ones, each with an outside witness. Send a draft of section one to someone by 4pm today. Book a 20-minute review for tomorrow morning. Consequence now beats consequence later.
cards.depth: Medication shifts the curve for some people but does not remove it. Checkpoints should be small, dated, and visible to another person, since a private promise has no one to discount against. Judge each by whether it changes what you do in the next two hours.

cards.hook: SAG's 1960 strike traded past residuals for a pension fund.
cards.body: In 1960 the Screen Actors Guild, led by Ronald Reagan, struck over payment when films were released to television. The studios argued that pre-1960 pictures had been made under contracts that did not reserve those rights. The settlement gave actors no residuals on that backlog. Instead, the studios paid a lump sum, reported at roughly 2.25 million dollars, into the guild's **pension and welfare fund**. Residuals applied only to later films. The guild chose a durable institution over a one-time payout to individuals.
cards.depth: The same structure recurs in streaming-era bargaining: a new exhibition window is monetized by converting backlog claims into fund contributions, with per-use payments applying only to future work. When reading any new residual formula, ask which cohort got the cash and which got the fund.

cards.hook: Your delta-hedged P&L depends on realized minus implied variance.
cards.body: A delta-hedged long option earns roughly **half gamma times spot squared times the gap between realized and implied variance**, per unit of time. Direction drops out. What remains is a bet on squared moves, weighted by dollar gamma. Dollar gamma peaks at the money and near expiry, so the same vol miss pays far more there than in a wing. That is how you can be right that vol is cheap and still lose: the variance arrived while spot sat far from your strike, where your gamma was small.
cards.depth: The formula holds per period when the option is valued at its implied vol, which is why implied vol is your breakeven, not your forecast. The result is path-dependent. Two paths with identical realized vol can produce different P&L depending on where spot spent its time relative to the strike.

cards.hook: Trade the plateau of your parameter sweep, not its peak.
cards.body: A parameter sweep gives you a surface. **Choose the center of the broad plateau**, not the highest cell. If a 20-day lookback shows a Sharpe of 1.4 but 18 and 22 days show 0.6, you have not found an edge. You have found noise that happened to line up. A real effect degrades smoothly as you nudge its inputs, because the underlying behavior does not care about your exact number. The peak is also where selection bias is largest, since you picked the maximum of many noisy draws. The plateau is the part of the surface you can still believe out of sample.
cards.depth: Practical check: plot the metric across each parameter pair and look for a wide, flat region. Then size the live position off the plateau's average, not its best cell. If no plateau exists anywhere on the surface, the strategy is the problem, not the parameter.

cards.hook: Ninety-five percent confidence, right 70% of the time, loses to 50/50.
cards.body: Brier score is squared error: forecast minus outcome, squared, where the outcome is 0 or 1. A constant 50% forecast scores 0.25 every time. Now take a forecaster who says 95% on everything and is right only 70% of the time. Expected score: 0.7 x 0.0025 plus 0.3 x 0.9025, about 0.27. **Overconfidence at that level is worse than a coin flip.** The quadratic penalty means a confident miss costs about 0.90, while a confident hit saves at most 0.25 versus a coin flip. The asymmetry punishes the wrong kind of conviction.
cards.depth: Lower is better. This is why proper scoring rules matter: they make honest probabilities the best strategy. The practical move is to track your hit rate at each confidence level and shade your stated numbers toward it before you act.

cards.hook: Fin-syn rules made networks rent shows they were forbidden to own.
cards.body: The FCC's financial interest and syndication rules, adopted in 1970 and effective in 1971, barred the three networks from taking syndication rights or equity in shows produced by outsiders, and from domestic syndication themselves. So **studios kept the back end** while networks held only a license window. That produced deficit financing: studios licensed episodes below cost, then recouped in syndication. The rules were largely relaxed in 1993 and then phased out by 1995. Networks promptly bought or built studios. Streaming platforms are now doing the same thing at larger scale.
cards.depth: Notice the rhyme with the Paramount decrees: both rules separated distribution from production, and both vanished when a new distribution technology made the old structure look quaint. The back end is where the leverage always was, and it is why talent deals still fight over ownership.

cards.hook: More stimulant is not more focus; the dose-response is an inverted U.
cards.body: Prefrontal working memory depends on catecholamine signaling being in a middle range. Too little norepinephrine and dopamine impairs it, and too much impairs it as well. Preclinical work from Arnsten and colleagues describes this as an inverted U. Mid-titration, the practical implication is that **more drug can feel like focus while working memory actually degrades**. Overshoot tends to look like tunnel vision on the wrong task, difficulty switching away, jitter, or flattened affect, rather than a dramatic high.
cards.depth: Concrete move: during titration, test flexibility, not output. Note whether you can drop a task when the calendar says to, and hold three items in mind without writing them down. Bring those observations to your prescriber. Dose decisions are theirs; the data is yours to collect.

cards.hook: Pin risk is a weekend gap you chose to hold.
cards.body: When a short equity option expires with the stock sitting at your strike, you cannot know whether you will be assigned. Holders can decide on exercise after the closing bell, so the answer arrives after the market has shut. If you guess wrong, you walk into Monday with **a stock position you never intended**, plus whatever news landed over the weekend. Hedging on Friday against an assignment that may not come leaves you either naked or doubly long. The cleanest fix is mechanical: close or roll any short strike within a hair of the close before expiration day ends, and pay the spread to avoid the coin flip.
cards.depth: Cash-settled index options sidestep this, since there is no stock to be delivered. The risk is concentrated in single names and ETFs. Positions that look flat on paper at 4pm can be exposed through the weekend, which is why the cost of closing is usually cheaper than it feels.

cards.hook: Autocorrelated returns make an annualized Sharpe lie.
cards.body: The standard move is multiplying a monthly Sharpe by the square root of 12. That formula assumes returns are independent month to month. If your strategy has positive autocorrelation, as with **smoothed marks, stale prices, or short-option books that bleed slowly**, the true annual volatility is higher than the naive scaling implies, so the annualized Sharpe is overstated. Andrew Lo's 2002 paper on the topic reported overstatement of up to roughly 65% for some hedge fund return series. Before trusting any annualized Sharpe, compute the first-order autocorrelation of your returns. If it is meaningfully positive, rescale using the actual annual-horizon variance.
cards.depth: Illiquid assets and strategies priced from stale quotes are the usual culprits. A quick check: compare the Sharpe computed on monthly returns with one computed on non-overlapping annual returns. A big gap points to serial correlation hiding in the data.

cards.hook: Calibrate time with your own ratio, not effort.
cards.body: Time estimation is a documented weak point in ADHD, and research reports larger errors in judging and reproducing durations than in controls. Willpower does not fix an internal clock, so replace the clock with data. For ten tasks, write the estimate before starting, then log the actual time. Divide actual by estimate for each task and take the median. That is **your personal multiplier**. If it comes out at 2.0, every future estimate gets doubled before it goes on the calendar. The move is the same one Kahneman prescribed for planning fallacy: stop consulting your inside view and consult your own reference class.
cards.depth: Track by task type, since your multiplier for email may differ from the one for drafting. Review the ratio monthly. A shifting multiplier during titration is useful information to bring to the prescriber, because it is an observed number rather than a feeling.

cards.hook: Give subagents the question, not the conversation.
cards.body: Forwarding a full parent context to a subagent feels safe, but it defeats the reason to spawn one. The parent's context window is the scarce resource, and a subagent exists to **spend its own context so the parent does not have to**. Hand it a brief instead: the goal, constraints, what done looks like, and the output format. Require a compact return, such as findings with file paths, not a transcript of the search. A good test: if you could not hand this brief to a contractor with no access to your chat, the subagent will also guess at what you meant.
cards.depth: Failure mode on the return side: a subagent that reports confident conclusions without evidence forces the parent to either trust blindly or redo the work. Ask for citations to specific locations so verification costs seconds.

cards.hook: Recall it: why did Midler's voice claim dodge copyright preemption?
cards.body: Think about what preemption actually requires before you answer. The Copyright Act only preempts state claims that fall within the subject matter of copyright. Bette Midler's sound-alike case in the Ninth Circuit, decided in 1988, turned on exactly that: **a voice is not a copyrightable work**, so her state-law claim was never inside the preemption zone. Waits v. Frito-Lay followed in 1992. The very thing that denies a voice copyright protection is what leaves it open to state right-of-publicity and misappropriation theories.
cards.depth: It matters again because synthetic-voice claims are routinely framed as copyright problems when the stronger theory is often state publicity law. The preemption defense is weakest precisely where the identity, not a recording, is the thing taken.

cards.hook: SPX options tax a short-term gain at a blended 26.8%.
cards.body: SPX options are Section 1256 contracts. 60% of any gain is taxed as long-term and 40% as short-term, whatever the holding period. At top federal rates that is 0.6 x 20% + 0.4 x 37%, a blended **26.8%**, against 37% on a one-day SPY trade in a taxable account. Positions are also marked to market on December 31. On a strategy netting 15% pre-tax, that 10.2 point rate gap is worth roughly 1.5 points of return a year. Cash settlement also removes assignment risk.
cards.depth: The same treatment applies to losses, and a net 1256 loss can be carried back three years against prior 1256 gains. The wash sale rule does not apply to these contracts. The cost is the year-end mark: unrealized gains are taxed whether or not you closed.

cards.hook: Overlapping labels leak your test set into training.
cards.body: Say your label is a 10-day forward return. Row t and row t+1 share nine days of the same price path, so they are nearly the same observation. Random k-fold puts one in training and the other in test, and the model scores well by **memorizing neighbors**. The fix is purging: drop any training row whose label window overlaps the test fold. Then add an embargo gap after the test fold to catch serial correlation in the features. Without both, your out-of-sample number is partly in-sample.
cards.depth: Purged k-fold with an embargo is laid out in Marcos Lopez de Prado's Advances in Financial Machine Learning. A practical starting embargo is about the label horizon, longer if your features are slow moving averages.

cards.hook: The auction winner is usually the one who overestimated most.
cards.body: Suppose ten bidders each estimate a common-value asset with unbiased noise. The winner is whoever's error was most positive, so the winning bid lands above true value even though every estimate was fair. This is the **winner's curse**. It gets worse as bidders are added and as estimates get noisier. The rational correction is to shade your bid below your estimate, by more when you face more competitors. It applies to any bidding war where everyone reads the same noisy comps, like a hot package or spec script.
cards.depth: Capen, Clapp and Campbell argued in 1971 that Gulf of Mexico oil lease bidders earned below-expected returns, a claim later debated. Lab experiments by Kagel and Levin found that inexperienced bidders routinely overbid in common-value auctions.

cards.hook: Breakfast can delay your lisdexamfetamine peak by about an hour.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine converts to dextroamphetamine after absorption, but food still moves the peak. Per the label, a high-fat meal pushes time to peak back by roughly an hour, while total exposure stays about the same. So during titration, **a consistent breakfast time** matters more than what the breakfast is. If onset on Tuesday arrives later than Monday, check when and what you ate before you conclude the dose behaved differently.
cards.depth: Add a meal timestamp to your dose timestamp and your first-focused-work timestamp. Three clocks plus one meal line make the pattern readable. Take it to your prescriber as data; don't adjust the dose yourself on one day's reading.

cards.hook: In audio, a room doesn't exist until you hear it.
cards.body: Film gets an establishing shot for free. Audio fiction gets nothing, so the listener builds the room only from sound. Give every new location **one anchoring sound** within the first few seconds: a specific footstep surface, a distinctive reverb, a machine hum that only exists there. Then reuse that sound when you return, and the listener relocates instantly without a line of narration. Name the place in dialogue only if the sound can't carry it. Narrated scene-setting is the weakest tool you have.
cards.depth: Test it by muting your dialogue track and listening to the ambience alone. If you can't tell the kitchen from the car, the listener can't either. Change the room tone, not the script.

cards.hook: Your SPX monthly stopped trading a session before it expired.
cards.body: Standard SPX monthly options expire on the third Friday, but they are AM-settled. Trading stops at Thursday's close, and the settlement value comes from the **opening prices** of the index constituents on Friday. The weekly SPXW series is PM-settled, so two contracts can share an expiration date and still be different instruments. If you hold a monthly spread into expiry, you carry a full overnight gap that you cannot trade out of in the option. A futures or ETF hedge is a different exposure with its own basis. Pin risk is murkier too, because the final settle is not any price you saw trade.
cards.depth: Check the root symbol and settlement style before you roll or close. Same date, different cutoff. VIX options have a similar quirk: they settle on a special opening quotation built from SPX option prices on Wednesday morning, not on a traded VIX print.

cards.hook: Recall it: why do 100 junk strategies yield a 1.3 Sharpe?
cards.body: Hint: the standard error of a zero-skill Sharpe over five years is about 0.45, and you ran 100 trials. The best of N noise draws sits roughly sigma times the square root of 2 ln N above zero. That is about three standard errors, or a Sharpe near 1.3. The answer is **selection, not skill**. The winner is the luckiest noise in your search space, so the number of variants you tried, including the ones you discarded, is part of the result.
cards.depth: Report the trial count next to every Sharpe. Without it the number cannot be interpreted, and it is exactly the input a deflated Sharpe calculation needs.

cards.hook: Investors realize gains about 1.5 times as often as losses.
cards.body: Terrance Odean's 1998 study of a discount brokerage's accounts found that investors sold winners at a much higher rate than losers. Reported figures were roughly 15% of paper gains realized against roughly 10% of paper losses. Loss aversion makes closing a loser feel like **crystallizing the mistake**, so the position stays open. It is also backwards on taxes, since realized losses are the ones that are useful. Odean reported that the winners people sold went on to beat the losers they kept. For a trader the fix is mechanical: decide the exit before entry, so the position never gets a vote.
cards.depth: The tell in your own book is holding period. If your average losing trade lasts longer than your average winner, the disposition effect is probably running your exits. Pull the numbers once a quarter.

cards.hook: A tool's error message is a prompt to the agent.
cards.body: When a tool fails, the model reads the error text and decides what to do next. A bare "400 Bad Request" gives it nothing to work with, so it retries the same call or invents a workaround. An error that says **what was wrong and what a valid call looks like** lets it self-correct in one step. Name the offending parameter, state the accepted format or range, and suggest the nearest valid option. Treat every error string as part of your prompt surface. It is the one piece of instruction the agent is guaranteed to read at the exact moment it is confused.
cards.depth: Test it by replaying failures. Feed your actual error strings to a fresh model with only the tool schema and see if it fixes the call. If it cannot, a person reading the log will struggle too.

cards.hook: Hollywood sued over the VCR, then earned more from it than theaters.
cards.body: Universal and Disney sued Sony in 1976 over the Betamax. Jack Valenti told Congress in 1982 that the VCR was to the film industry what the Boston strangler was to a woman home alone. The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 for Sony in 1984. It held that home time-shifting was fair use and that selling a device **capable of substantial noninfringing uses** was not contributory infringement. Within a few years, home video revenue rivaled and then passed theatrical rentals for the studios. The technology they tried to enjoin became their largest profit center.
cards.depth: The Sony standard still frames tool-maker liability fights, from Grokster in 2005 to AI cases today. Statutes like Tennessee's ELVIS Act are partly a reaction to it, because they target a tool's primary purpose rather than its capacity for lawful use.

cards.hook: Dispersion trades profit from selling correlation, not volatility.
cards.body: Index options are bought as portfolio insurance, so index implied vol carries a bid that single-stock options lack. The gap shows up as implied correlation sitting above the correlation that later realizes. A dispersion trade shorts index variance and buys component variance, which makes you **short correlation**, not short volatility. You collect when stocks move on their own stories. You lose when a macro shock pushes every name the same way at once.
cards.depth: Correlation is the unhedged tail. In selloffs, realized correlation jumps toward one, so the long component legs fail to offset the short index leg exactly when it matters. Treat it as a short-gamma book with a hidden crash exposure, and size it for that.

cards.hook: Your backtest assumes your order didn't move the price.
cards.body: Market impact empirically follows roughly a square-root law: cost scales with volatility times the square root of order size over daily volume. Double your size and impact rises about 41 percent, not 100. That sounds gentle, but it creates a **capacity ceiling**, the size where marginal impact eats marginal alpha. A backtest with fixed one-lot fills hides this completely, which is why a small-account Sharpe of 2 often fails to scale.
cards.depth: For options, the analog is quoted size at the touch and spreads widening as you work the order. Estimate capacity by rerunning with fills at the bid or ask plus a size-dependent penalty, then find the notional where net Sharpe halves.

cards.hook: XIV had to buy volatility after volatility had already doubled.
cards.body: On February 5, 2018, the VIX roughly doubled in a day, closing near 37 from about 17. XIV and similar inverse-volatility products were short VIX futures, and their rules required rebalancing at the close to restore their exposure. After a doubling, restoring that exposure meant buying futures at the day's worst prices, into the very rally that was hurting them. That **forced same-direction buying** fed the spike. XIV reportedly fell roughly 90 percent or more after hours and was then terminated.
cards.depth: The lesson is structural: a product whose mechanical rebalance runs in the direction of the move is short gamma at scale. Sponsors reportedly had an acceleration trigger tied to a very large one-day drop in indicative value, and it was hit.

cards.hook: Keep a parking-lot note open before you start.
cards.body: Mid-task, a stray thought (check that invoice, reply to that text) competes for working memory. Acting on it costs a task switch you then pay to reverse. The move: open one plain file titled Parking Lot before you begin. When an urge arrives, type five words and return to the task. This **offloads working memory** without obeying the impulse, and the capture gives the thought somewhere trustworthy to live. Review the list only at a planned break.
cards.depth: This is externalizing, not suppression; pushing a thought away is the weaker move. Keep the file one keystroke from where you work. If the list is never reviewed, the system decays, so attach review to a fixed stop point like lunch, not to a feeling.

cards.hook: A toddler's pointing at 14 months predicts later vocabulary.
cards.body: In a well-cited study by Rowe and Goldin-Meadow, the number of distinct things children pointed to at 14 months predicted their vocabulary at about 54 months. It also helped explain the vocabulary gap between higher and lower income households, because parents who gestured more had children who gestured more. The practical move is cheap: **name what they point to**. Point, label it in a short phrase, and let them point again.
cards.depth: The proposed mechanism is that gesture lets a child pick the topic before they have the words, so the parent supplies the translation at the exact moment attention is joined. It is a correlational finding with a plausible path, not proof that pointing drills build vocabulary.

cards.hook: A 30-delta put is not a 30% chance of loss.
cards.body: Delta is a rough proxy for the **risk-neutral probability** of finishing in the money, not the real-world one. Risk-neutral pricing bakes in the volatility risk premium: implied vol has historically exceeded subsequent realized vol on average for index options, and equities drift upward. So the real-world chance that a 30-delta index put finishes in the money is typically lower than 30%. That gap is why selling puts wins often. It is also the premium for bearing a tail where losses are large and clustered. A high win rate is the price of that payoff shape, not proof of skill.
cards.depth: Strictly, delta is N(d1) while the risk-neutral in-the-money probability is N(d2) for a call, or N(-d2) for a put. They differ by a term that grows with vol and time. The cleaner read of risk-neutral odds is the slope of option price against strike, scaled by the discount factor.

cards.hook: Daily bars can't tell you if your stop or target hit first.
cards.body: When a daily bar's range touches both your stop and your profit target, the bar does not record which came first. Backtests that quietly assume the target fills first, or that use the close, **resolve the ambiguity in your favor**. The error is largest for tight brackets on volatile days, and it makes tight-stop, tight-target strategies look better than they are. Fix it by assuming the worst order on ambiguous bars, or by replaying those days on intraday data. If the result only survives under the optimistic ordering, you were measuring the assumption.
cards.depth: Count how many trades hit both levels inside a single bar. If it is more than a few percent of trades, the ordering rule is effectively a parameter, and you should report results under both orderings. The same logic applies to limit orders that were touched but not necessarily filled, since queue position decides those.

cards.hook: SAG-AFTRA treats a synthetic performer differently from a digital replica.
cards.body: In the 2023 TV/theatrical agreement, a digital replica of a real performer needs **informed consent with a reasonably specific description** of intended use, plus compensation. A synthetic performer, an AI-generated figure not recognizable as any particular human, is handled through notice to the union and an opportunity to bargain, not individual consent. The seam is the composite: a synthetic that resembles a real performer's face or voice is arguably a replica in disguise, and the text gives no clean answer. Draft for that seam, because the lookalike dispute will land there.
cards.depth: Talent side: add a representation that no synthetic is trained on or tuned to the client's likeness without consent. Production side: document generation provenance. Check the current cycle's terms, since these agreements get renegotiated and the 2023 text may have been updated.

cards.hook: Rereading feels like learning. Testing yourself actually is.
cards.body: In Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 study, students read a prose passage and then either restudied it or took recall tests. Five minutes later, restudying won. A week later, **testing beat restudying**, with roughly 60% retained versus about 40%. Rereading creates fluency, the feeling that material is familiar, and fluency is a poor proxy for retrievable memory. Effortful retrieval strengthens the route back to the memory itself. The move: after reading anything you need, close it, write what you remember, then check. The ugly feeling of not remembering is the part that works.
cards.depth: The benefit is largest when retrieval is hard but still succeeds, and when feedback afterward corrects errors. Spacing multiplies it. This is the logic behind the callback cards in this feed.

cards.hook: Recall it: why did a precise opening number outperform a round one?
cards.body: Think about what the other side infers when they see $79,300 instead of $80,000. Take a beat. The answer: they read precision as **evidence of homework**, so they adjust less. In Mason, Lee, Wiley, and Ames (2013), precise openers drew counteroffers that stayed closer to the opening number than round ones did. Round numbers invite haggling in round steps. Precise numbers signal a basis whether or not one exists. The move: build your opening figure from components you can name, then state it unrounded.
cards.depth: Worth retrieving again before your next first offer. The failure mode is precision without a basis: a sharp counterparty will ask how you got there, and a number you cannot decompose collapses faster than a round one.

cards.hook: A deep in-the-money put is worth more dead than alive.
cards.body: An American put can be exercised any time, so it never trades below intrinsic value. Deep in the money, its remaining optionality is tiny, because the stock has little room to fall further. Exercising converts the stock into **strike cash that earns interest starting today**. When that interest exceeds the leftover time value, holding is the mistake. Higher rates pull the early-exercise boundary closer to the money. This is the mirror image of the call-and-dividend case, with the carry running the other way.
cards.depth: A European put has no such floor: it can trade below K minus S, because the strike arrives only at expiry. Dividends work against early put exercise, since the ex-date drop in the stock helps the put holder who waits.

cards.hook: A voice isn't copyrightable, which is why it's protectable.
cards.body: Practitioners often assume copyright preemption will sink a voice-clone claim. The Ninth Circuit rejected that logic decades before generative AI. In Midler v. Ford (1988), an ad agency hired a sound-alike after Bette Midler declined. The court held that a **voice is not a copyrightable work**, so the Copyright Act did not preempt her state-law claim. Waits v. Frito-Lay (1992) followed the same path. Preemption only applies to rights within the subject matter of copyright, and a vocal identity sits outside it. The synthetic-voice cases are built on this foundation.
cards.depth: The caveat is that outcomes turn on state law. Midler rested on California common-law misappropriation, and statutes like Tennessee's ELVIS Act now codify voice rights. A defendant's best argument is usually not preemption but First Amendment or lack of identifiability.

cards.hook: Perfect calibration can still make you a useless forecaster.
cards.body: Say it rains on 30% of days, and you forecast 30% every single day. You are perfectly calibrated: of your 30% calls, 30% come true. You are also worthless, because the forecast never changes with the situation. The Murphy decomposition splits the Brier score into reliability (calibration), resolution, and uncertainty. **Resolution is the part that rewards discrimination**: pushing forecasts away from the base rate when the evidence warrants it. A good forecaster needs both, and most calibration training only teaches the first.
cards.depth: Brier = reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty, where uncertainty is fixed by the base rate. Your score improves only by lowering reliability error or raising resolution. Check which one you are actually moving.

cards.hook: Lisdexamfetamine is inactive until your blood cells cut it.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug: dextroamphetamine bonded to the amino acid lysine. It does nothing until enzymes, mainly in red blood cells, cleave the bond. That makes activation **rate-limited by hydrolysis, not by your stomach**, which is why onset feels slower and smoother than immediate-release, with dextroamphetamine peaking roughly 3.5 hours after the dose. The concrete move: do not judge a dose by the first hour. Feeling nothing at 45 minutes is the expected pharmacology, not a failed dose.
cards.depth: Because activation does not depend on gastric pH, food mainly delays the peak slightly rather than changing the total. Duration is reported at roughly 10 to 14 hours, so dosing time matters for sleep. This is a good reason to log timestamps for your prescriber.

cards.hook: If a scene ends where it began, cut it.
cards.body: Robert McKee's test for a scene is simple: it must turn a value. Name the value at the opening in one word (safe, trusting, winning) and again at the close. If both words match, you wrote a transition, not a scene. **The turn must be the point of the scene**, not a side effect of it. For audio fiction this matters more, because the listener has no visual cut to reset attention. The turn has to land as a line, a sound, or a silence the listener can hear.
cards.depth: Run it as an edit pass on any script: write the opening and closing value next to each scene heading. Runs of three or more identical pairs mark the sag. Merge those scenes or give one of them a reversal.

cards.hook: Calls get exercised early only when the dividend beats time value.
cards.body: American calls on dividend payers are almost never exercised early, with one exception: the session before the ex-dividend date. The holder rationally exercises only when **the dividend exceeds the call's remaining extrinsic value**. A deep in-the-money call with a few cents of extrinsic and a dividend on the calendar is the candidate. If you are short that call, overnight assignment leaves you short stock going into the ex-date, and you owe the dividend. So before every ex-date, scan your short calls for extrinsic value below the dividend.
cards.depth: Exercising early also forfeits interest on the strike cash you would otherwise hold, which raises the hurdle slightly. Short call spreads are the classic trap: the short leg gets assigned overnight while the long leg stays unexercised, leaving you with unwanted stock and margin exposure.

cards.hook: Signal at the close, fill at the close: a quiet look-ahead.
cards.body: A signal computed from today's close cannot be traded at today's close. The close is only known once it prints, yet many backtests compute on a bar and fill at that same bar's price. It is look-ahead bias in its quietest form. The damage concentrates in **short-horizon reversal and breakout signals**, where the last tick drives both the signal and the fill. The fix is mechanical: lag the signal one bar and fill at the next open, or at the next close if you trade the auction. If the edge shrinks sharply, it was partly borrowed from the future.
cards.depth: Test it directly: shift your signal one bar later and rerun. A real edge decays gently with delay. A phantom edge collapses. Plotting performance against 0, 1, 2 and 3 bars of lag is a cheap robustness curve most backtests never produce.

cards.hook: California voids vague digital-replica clauses unless the performer had counsel.
cards.body: California's AB 2602, effective January 1, 2025, makes a contract provision unenforceable if it lets a company create and use a digital replica of a performer's voice or likeness in place of work they would otherwise have done in person. The trigger is twofold: the provision lacks a **reasonably specific description of the intended uses**, and the performer was not represented by counsel or a union. Boilerplate like "all media now known or hereafter devised" is exactly what the statute targets. Practitioners drafting replica grants should list the uses and document representation.
cards.depth: The contested edge is scope: whether a general grant reaches a replica performing work the individual never would have done is less clear. Treat the statute as a floor for specificity, not a safe harbor, and expect guild terms to set a higher bar for covered performers.

cards.hook: Swap the clock for a shrinking visual countdown.
cards.body: Time blindness in ADHD shows up in research as impaired time estimation and reproduction, not mere lateness. A numeric clock demands that you convert digits into elapsed time, which is exactly the step that fails. A **shrinking visual countdown** turns remaining time into an area you can see, like a red disc or a draining bar. Set it for the work block, not the deadline, and put it in your line of sight. You are not trying to feel time better. You are moving the computation out of your head and onto the desk.
cards.depth: A passive countdown can still be ignored in hyperfocus, so add an audible alarm at the end, plus a travel buffer if the next commitment is offsite. Run it for a week and keep whichever cue actually got you moving.

cards.hook: Recall it: what rule change broke the Hunt brothers' silver squeeze?
cards.body: Nudge: the position was legal, but the rulebook was not fixed. In early 1980, COMEX imposed **position limits and liquidation-only trading** in silver. The Hunts could no longer add to the position propping up the price, while margin calls on the existing one kept coming. Silver fell from roughly $50 in January to around $11 on March 27, 1980, Silver Thursday. The exchange rewrote the rules while the squeeze was live.
cards.depth: Any strategy leaning on a venue's rules, such as squeezes, pinned expiries, or margin regimes, carries rule-change risk that no backtest prices. Ask who can edit the rulebook, and what they gain by doing it mid-game.

cards.hook: A hard-to-borrow stock makes puts expensive without anyone being bearish.
cards.body: Put-call parity pins calls, puts, and the forward. The forward is spot plus carry, minus dividends, minus the **borrow fee** that shorts pay. When a stock is hard to borrow, the forward drops, so puts price above calls at the same strike. A synthetic long looks cheap and a synthetic short looks rich. That skew on a heavily shorted name can be pure financing, not fear. Back out the implied borrow rate from parity before you read a bearish signal into the chain.
cards.depth: Back out the forward from the strike where call and put mids match: F = K + e^(rT)(C - P). Then borrow is roughly r - q - ln(F/S)/T. Use near-ATM, short-dated quotes. American early-exercise premium contaminates single-stock puts, so treat the result as an estimate.

cards.hook: Try 100 useless strategies for five years; the best shows Sharpe 1.3.
cards.body: With five years of data, the annualized Sharpe of a zero-skill strategy has a standard error near 0.45. The best of N independent trials sits roughly sigma times the square root of 2 ln N above zero. For N = 100 that is about three standard errors, so a Sharpe near 1.3 appears from **pure selection**. The backtest did not find an edge. It found the luckiest noise in your search space. Count every variant you tried, including the ones you discarded, and demand the winner clear that bar.
cards.depth: This is the logic behind the deflated Sharpe ratio (Bailey and Lopez de Prado). It also assumes independent trials. Correlated variants lower the effective N, but you rarely know by how much, so log your trial count honestly.

cards.hook: Tennessee's ELVIS Act can reach the tool maker, not just the user.
cards.body: Most practitioners read digital-replica statutes as targeting whoever publishes the fake. Tennessee's ELVIS Act, effective July 1, 2024, goes further. It adds liability for distributing or making available an algorithm, software, or tool whose **primary purpose** is producing an unauthorized likeness or voice. It also protects voice as such, including simulations, not just recordings of the actual person. The risk analysis for a voice-cloning vendor or a studio's AI tool licensor therefore starts at the product's stated purpose, not at user misuse.
cards.depth: The 'primary purpose' test is untested in reported decisions as far as I know. Marketing copy and onboarding flows are likely evidence, so vendor reps and indemnities should be drafted around how the product is described, not just how it is used.

cards.hook: Schedule your hardest task for hours three to four after dosing.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug. It has to be converted to dextroamphetamine in red blood cells before it does anything. The prodrug itself peaks around an hour after the dose, but the active d-amphetamine peaks roughly **three to four hours** in. That means the first hour is a poor slot for your most demanding work, and the mid-morning window is the best one. Put the task that needs sustained inhibition and working memory there. Put email and admin on either side of it.
cards.depth: Timing varies by person, food, and dose. Mid-titration, check this against your own timestamps instead of the average curve. The point is to place the demanding task by where your own peak lands.

cards.hook: The 1948 Paramount decrees lasted 72 years.
cards.body: The Supreme Court ruled against the major studios in 1948, and consent decrees followed that forced them to divest their theater chains. They also banned block booking and circuit dealing. The decrees were meant to restore competition, but they outlived the industry they described. The Justice Department moved to terminate them in 2019, and a federal judge ended them in August 2020 with a **two-year sunset** on block booking and circuit dealing. A rule written for 1940s exhibition governed streaming-era distribution until then.
cards.depth: The rhyme is with fin-syn, which was also an antitrust remedy and was repealed in the mid-1990s. Both show how long structural remedies persist after the facts that justified them have changed.

cards.hook: A variance swap hands you convexity you didn't ask for.
cards.body: A variance swap pays notional times (realized variance minus strike variance). Variance is vol squared, so the payoff is convex in vol. Say the strike is 20. Realized vol of 30 pays about 12.5 vol points of vega notional. Realized vol of 10 costs you about 7.5. Same 10-point miss either way, unequal result. The long side owns **free convexity in volatility**, so the seller charges for it. The variance strike sits above the equivalent vol swap strike, and by more when skew is steep. Quote it as a straight vol bet and you misprice the exact thing you are buying.
cards.depth: Replication explains the skew link. A variance swap is a strip of options weighted by 1/K squared, which loads heavily on far downside puts. So its strike embeds the tail. Vega notional is conventionally set as variance notional times 2K, which linearizes the payoff at the strike. Short variance is the purest bet that the tail never shows up.

cards.hook: The Copyright Office won't register prompts, but will register your arrangement.
cards.body: Practitioners keep saying AI-assisted work is unprotectable. That is too blunt. The Copyright Office's January 2025 report concluded that prompts alone do not give enough control to make the user an author. But **human-authored elements still register**: your own text, your modifications to output, and your selection and arrangement. The 2023 Zarya of the Dawn decision showed the split. The comic's text and layout were registered, while the Midjourney images were not. The real work is documentation: keep drafts, edits, and the human choices that shaped the final asset, because the claim will need to be itemized.
cards.depth: Applicants must disclose AI-generated material that is more than de minimis and disclaim it in the registration. Omitting the disclosure risks invalidating the registration later. For chain-of-title diligence, ask for the generation and edit history, not just a rep that the work is original.

cards.hook: Kahneman's team guessed two years. Comparable teams took seven to ten.
cards.body: Kahneman describes a curriculum project he worked on in which each team member estimated roughly two years. He then asked the curriculum expert, Seymour Fox, how similar teams had fared. Fox said about 40% never finished, and the ones that did took seven to ten years. Kahneman's project took about eight. **The outside view** starts from the distribution of comparable cases, not from your plan. The team had the base rate in the room and ignored it until someone asked. Ask the reference-class question first. Then adjust for what makes you different, and be honest that it is usually less than you think.
cards.depth: The inside view builds a scenario step by step, and every step feels plausible, so the total feels safe. That is the planning fallacy. The fix is mechanical: pick a reference class, take its median and spread, then adjust a little. Apply it to a production schedule or a trade's holding period the same way.

cards.hook: Your 3pm coffee is still half-present at bedtime.
cards.body: Caffeine's half-life averages roughly five to six hours in healthy adults, with wide individual variation. So a 200 mg dose at 3pm leaves about 100 mg circulating near 9pm. It works by blocking adenosine receptors, which does not erase sleep pressure. It just masks it. A well-known 2013 lab study (Drake and colleagues) found that 400 mg taken six hours before bed measurably cut sleep time. Participants did not feel the loss. **Perceived sleep disruption understates the measured loss**, so your gut is a poor judge here. Since you track sleep, run the test on your own data: cutoff at noon for two weeks, then compare.
cards.depth: Half-life varies with genetics (CYP1A2), smoking, hormonal contraceptives, and pregnancy. Change one variable at a time, otherwise your Oura trend line will blame the wrong thing. Judge by deep sleep and resting heart rate over weeks, not a single night.

cards.hook: Recall it: what ratio decides whether a signal survives its costs?
cards.body: Think of a signal earning 6 bps gross per round trip, with 3 bps of round-trip costs. Half the edge is gone before slippage error. Retrieve the ratio before reading on. It is the **break-even cost multiple**: gross edge divided by round-trip cost, here 2x. That, not Sharpe, tells you how much execution error you can absorb. Below 2x, assume live trading kills it. Then multiply by turnover: daily trading pays costs about 20 times as often as monthly.
cards.depth: It matters again because options spreads are wide in percentage terms and widen in stress, exactly when your signal fires hardest. Re-run any backtest at double the assumed cost. If the edge disappears, you never had a margin of safety.

cards.hook: An ATM straddle prices a 0.8 sigma move, not one sigma.
cards.body: An ATM straddle does not price a one-sigma move. It prices the **expected absolute move, roughly 0.8 sigma**, because the mean absolute deviation of a normal distribution is about 0.8 of its standard deviation. At 20% implied vol on a 30-day option, one sigma is about 5.7% of spot, while the straddle costs roughly 4.6%. So the 'implied move' people quote from a straddle is the typical size of a move, and a one-sigma move is a bigger event than that. Compare realized absolute moves to 0.8 sigma, not 1.
cards.depth: With real fat-tailed returns, the mean absolute deviation often falls below 0.8 sigma, so the ratio is not a constant. To back out the implied one-sigma move from a straddle, divide its price by roughly 0.8 and sanity check against the stock's own history.

cards.hook: Backtesting options at mid-price quietly hands you the spread.
cards.body: Backtesting options at mid-price gives you the bid-ask spread for free. A four-leg iron condor crosses four spreads on entry and four on exit. With a hypothetical **nickel of half-spread per leg**, that is 20 cents in and 20 out, or 40 cents round trip against a $1.50 credit, roughly 27% of the premium gone before any loss. Edge in short premium is often only a few percent a year, so friction of this size can erase it entirely. Spreads also widen in stress, which is exactly when you adjust.
cards.depth: Rerun the test with fills 25%, 50%, and 100% of the way from mid to the worse quote, and plot return against that fraction. If the curve crosses zero before 50%, your live fills will decide whether you have a strategy at all.

cards.hook: In 1952 the actors' union let a talent agency produce TV.
cards.body: In 1952 the Screen Actors Guild, led by Ronald Reagan, granted talent agency MCA a **blanket waiver** from the rule barring agents from producing. MCA's Revue Productions then made television shows starring its own clients, which put the agency on both sides of the table. It bought the Universal backlot in 1958, then Decca, Universal's parent, in 1962. Antitrust pressure from the Justice Department forced it to drop the agency business and keep the studio.
cards.depth: The same conflict resurfaced in the 2019 WGA fight with the major agencies over packaging fees and agency-affiliated production arms, and the 2020 agreements restricted agency-owned production. The 1962 split held for roughly sixty years.

cards.hook: Urine pH changes how fast amphetamine leaves your body.
cards.body: Amphetamine is a weak base, and how much of it is excreted unchanged depends on urine pH. **Acidic urine speeds clearance** and shortens the effect, while alkaline urine slows clearance and lengthens it. Prescribing labels list urinary acidifiers and alkalinizers, such as large doses of vitamin C or sodium bicarbonate, as interactions. The move: if a dose feels unusually short or long, add 'big vitamin C, antacid, or heavy citrus today?' to your timestamp log, and ask your prescriber before supplementing regularly.
cards.depth: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug converted to dextroamphetamine in red blood cells, so absorption is fairly insensitive to stomach acid. The excretion side is still pH-dependent. Treat it as one variable among several to rule out, not a dial to adjust yourself.

cards.hook: Show the bomb before the conversation. Suspense is information asymmetry.
cards.body: Hitchcock's famous example: two people talk at a table, and a bomb goes off. That is **15 seconds of surprise**. Show the audience the bomb under the table first, and the same ordinary conversation becomes 15 minutes of suspense, because they know what the characters do not. For audio fiction, the tool is a sound cue only the listener can interpret: a ticking, a lock turning, a second set of footsteps. Plant it in the first line of the scene, then let the dialogue stay mundane. The gap between what they know and what the characters know does the work.
cards.depth: Surprise gives a single jolt; suspense gives sustained attention. Use surprise sparingly for reveals and suspense for scenes you need the listener to lean into. Hitchcock described the bomb example in his interviews with Truffaut.

cards.hook: Full Kelly gives you a coin flip on halving your bankroll.
cards.body: In the continuous Kelly model, the probability that your wealth ever touches a fraction x of its starting level is exactly x. So full Kelly carries a 50% chance of halving at some point, and a 10% chance of falling to a tenth. That is the price of maximizing the growth rate. Bet a fraction f of Kelly and the odds of ever halving become 0.5 raised to the power (2/f minus 1). At half Kelly that is 12.5%, while you keep roughly 75% of the growth rate. **Fractional Kelly** is a drawdown purchase, not timidity.
cards.depth: The model assumes you know your edge. You never do, and estimated edges skew high after selection, so full Kelly on an estimated edge is usually an overbet. Sizing at half Kelly or below also absorbs that estimation error, which is why practitioners treat Kelly as a ceiling.

cards.hook: Recall it: why can averaging ten forecasters buy you nothing?
cards.body: Think about the identity behind the diversity prediction theorem. The crowd's squared error equals the average individual error minus one term. Which term? The **variance of the predictions**. If all ten read the same sources and share the same blind spot, that variance is near zero, so the crowd is exactly as wrong as the typical member. Averaging only helps when the errors point in different directions.
cards.depth: It matters again whenever you assemble a panel of analysts, models, or friends. Pick for different information and methods, not just top individual accuracy. Ask of any new member: what do they know or do differently that the rest of the panel does not?

cards.hook: Write the first physical action, not the task.
cards.body: A task like 'prep the negotiation outline' is not one step. Starting it forces you to plan, sequence, and choose, all executive-function work that raises the activation threshold before anything gets done. Pay that cost in advance, when you are calm, by rewriting the entry as a verb plus an object you can touch: 'open the term sheet, paste the three open issues into a blank page'. **The first action, not the project**, goes on the list. When the moment comes, the decision has already been made.
cards.depth: Test the wording: could you begin it with no further thought? If you still have to decide something, split the line again. Put it where you will see it at the moment of starting, such as the top of the doc or a sticky note on the screen.

cards.hook: A precise first offer anchors harder than a round one.
cards.body: In experiments by Mason, Lee, Wiley, and Ames (2013), negotiators who opened with precise figures like $79,300 rather than $80,000 got counteroffers that stayed closer to their number. Counterparties read precision as evidence of homework, so they adjust less and argue less. The effect appeared across several settings, including real estate pricing. A round number invites haggling in round steps. A **precise anchor** signals a basis, even when it has none. The practical move: build your opening figure from components you can name, then state it unrounded.
cards.depth: The caveat is that a precise number you cannot defend collapses on the first question about where it came from. Anchoring effects also shrink when the other side has done its own valuation, so use this most where information is thin.

cards.hook: Your LLM judge likes text that sounds like itself.
cards.body: Research on LLM evaluators has reported self-preference bias: a model rates its own outputs higher than equally good outputs from other sources, and the effect is linked to how familiar the text is to the model. If the same model writes and grades, your eval quietly rewards its own habits. The fix is structural. Use a **different model family as judge**, or a rubric with checkable criteria, and spot-check a sample against human grades. Treat any score from a same-model loop as optimistic until calibrated.
cards.depth: Judge-agreement with your own labels is the number to track. Hand-grade 30 to 50 outputs, compare, and rerun that comparison whenever you change the judge model or the rubric. A judge that cannot match you on that sample should not gate anything.

cards.hook: Your theta already tells you the daily move you need.
cards.body: For a delta-hedged option, daily theta decay and gamma P&L cancel exactly when the underlying moves by implied vol divided by the square root of 252. At 20% implied, that is roughly **a 1.26% daily move**. Anything smaller and the short-gamma seller keeps the decay. Anything larger and the long-gamma holder collects more than they paid. So every theta figure on your screen is really a price quote for one specific daily move, and your edge is the gap between that move and the one that actually shows up.
cards.depth: This is the Black-Scholes relation theta + 0.5 x gamma x S^2 x sigma^2 = 0 (rates ignored) in disguise. It holds per day only on average. Realized paths are lumpy, so the breakeven is a mean, not a guarantee, and gap days dominate the outcome.

cards.hook: A Sharpe of 1.0 over three years can still be zero.
cards.body: The standard error of an annualized Sharpe ratio is roughly the square root of (1 + half the Sharpe squared) divided by the years of data. For a Sharpe of 1.0 over three years, that is about 0.7. A 95% interval of **plus or minus 1.4** runs from slightly negative to above 2. Your backtest cannot distinguish a great strategy from a coin flip with a good streak. Before trusting a number, compute its error bar. Then ask how many years you would need to shrink that bar to something you could act on.
cards.depth: The formula assumes roughly independent, normal returns. Fat tails and autocorrelation, both common in short-premium strategies, make the true error bar wider. The result goes back to Andrew Lo's work on the statistics of Sharpe ratios.

cards.hook: Fair use covered the training. The pirated library copies didn't.
cards.body: In Bartz v. Anthropic (June 2025), Judge Alsup held that training on lawfully acquired books was fair use, calling it highly transformative. He refused to extend that to copies pulled from pirate sites and kept as a permanent library. That split opened **statutory damages exposure on acquisition**, not on training. The case then settled for a reported $1.5 billion, roughly $3,000 per work across about half a million books. The diligence question for any dataset is now where each copy came from, before it is what the model does with it.
cards.depth: Statutory damages run up to $150,000 per work for willful infringement, which is why class certification created settlement pressure. A district court ruling is not binding precedent, and other judges have weighed the market-harm factor differently. Treat it as a roadmap, not settled law.

cards.hook: During titration, log three timestamps, not how you feel.
cards.body: Mid-titration, how a dose feels is a poor guide. Stimulants can feel good at doses that hurt function, and rebound can masquerade as the drug failing. Record **onset, peak function, and the hour it fades**, each tied to a concrete output: when you started the first task, when you last finished something, when your focus fell off. Add appetite and bedtime. After a week, your prescriber sees a dose-response curve in your own data instead of a vague report that it was okay. Adjustments then rest on measurements, not mood.
cards.depth: Lisdexamfetamine is labeled to last roughly 12 to 14 hours in adults, but individual offset varies a lot. Bring the log to your prescriber, who decides dose changes. A phone note with three timestamps per day is enough.

cards.hook: The exchange changed the rules, and silver fell 80%.
cards.body: The Hunt brothers accumulated a huge silver position through 1979, helping push the price from roughly $6 to about $50 by January 1980. Then COMEX adopted position limits and a rule allowing liquidation-only trading. Buyers could no longer add, and margin calls kept coming. On March 27, 1980, Silver Thursday, they could not meet a reported margin call, and silver collapsed to around $11. The lesson is structural: **a squeeze depends on the rulebook**, and the party writing the rules can rewrite them against you at the worst moment.
cards.depth: The Hunts were later sued and fined, and Nelson Bunker Hunt filed for bankruptcy in 1988. Exact dates and figures vary by source, so treat the prices as approximate. The pattern recurs in the 2022 LME nickel episode, when the exchange canceled trades.

cards.hook: One vega in front month isn't one vega in back month.
cards.body: Raw vega adds across expiries, but implied vol does not move in parallel. Shocks hit the front hard and fade with maturity, so a 1-point jump in 30-day vol often arrives with a much smaller move in 120-day vol. A common fix is **time-weighted vega**: scale each expiry's vega by roughly the square root of (reference days divided by days to expiry). A calendar that looks vega-flat on the screen can still carry real front-month exposure, because the front leg is the part of the surface that actually moves.
cards.depth: The weighting is a rule of thumb, not a law. The true ratio shifts by regime: in a panic the whole curve inverts and front vol overshoots, while in quiet markets the back end barely stirs. Estimate your own term-structure beta from your underlying's history before trusting any single exponent.

cards.hook: Recall it: why distrust a parameter that beats its neighbors by far?
cards.body: Picture the peak you optimized. If the settings one step either side performed far worse, the winner was probably fitted noise. The payoff: **prefer a broad plateau over a sharp peak**. A 14-day lookback that shines while 13 and 15 collapse is not an edge. A robust strategy degrades gracefully when you nudge its settings, and live markets will nudge them for you through different spreads, fills, and regimes.
cards.depth: Run the sweep as a heat map, not a leaderboard. Pick the center of the largest flat, high region instead of the top cell, then check that the plateau survives a second asset or out-of-sample period. It pairs with multiple-testing bias: the more settings you try, the larger the luck share of the best one.

cards.hook: An MFN is only as good as its definition of 'better'.
cards.body: Most MFN fights are not about whether the clause exists. They are about the comparison. Term by term, or whole package? Same role, or any role? Same project, or the whole slate? Term-by-term lets the holder cherry-pick and ratchet, which is why payers resist it. Package-level comparison lets the payer **relabel value into a non-comparable form**, like a producer fee, a bonus, or a back-end definition. Whoever drafts the comparison basis controls what the MFN is worth.
cards.depth: Two practical tells: does the MFN carry a notice or audit right, and does it reach deals signed after yours? Without those, it is a promise nobody can verify. Holders should also ask whether the payer can sidestep it by routing economics through an affiliate.

cards.hook: Assume the trade already failed. Your reasons list gets longer.
cards.body: In a 1989 study, Mitchell, Russo and Pennington found that imagining an outcome as already having happened, called prospective hindsight, reportedly raised the ability to identify reasons for it by roughly 30%. The mechanism is simple. "It might fail" invites hedged, vague worry. "It did fail, why?" invites **a causal story**, and the mind is far better at explaining the past than forecasting the future. This is the logic behind Gary Klein's pre-mortem.
cards.depth: Run it before you size the position or sign the deal, not after. Write reasons privately first, then pool them, so the loudest voice does not anchor the list. The output is not a verdict. It is a list of specific failure paths you can monitor, hedge, or price.

cards.hook: Don't resist the distraction. Make it cost three extra steps.
cards.body: If inhibition is the weak link, a plan that depends on in-the-moment resistance is built on the weakest part. Use the environment instead. Delay discounting is hyperbolic, meaning the steepest drop in value comes at the **shortest delays**. So a tiny delay on the impulsive option cuts its pull far more than its size suggests. Log out after each use, pull the app off the home screen, and store the password in a manager you must open. Then do the reverse for the task you want: remove steps until starting takes one click.
cards.depth: This works because it changes the choice architecture, not your character. Add friction only to the two or three sinks that actually eat your hours, and re-check monthly. A workaround you stop noticing has decayed, and you will drift back to the old pattern.

cards.hook: Your delta is wrong if you assume the wrong skew dynamic.
cards.body: Black-Scholes delta assumes implied vol stays put as spot moves. In equity indexes it doesn't: spot falls, vol rises, and the correlation is strongly negative. So a put's real delta is **BS delta plus vega times the vol change per point of spot**, and that second term is also negative. Short a put and hedge with plain BS delta, and you are under-hedged exactly when it hurts: the spot loss and the vol gain on the option stack on the same side. Whether your model treats the smile as sticky-strike or sticky-delta quietly changes the number you trade.
cards.depth: Sticky-strike says each strike keeps its vol. Sticky-delta says vol follows moneyness, so the smile slides with spot. Index options usually sit between the two, and the balance shifts by regime. To see your gap, compare your broker's delta against a scenario reprice with a 1-point spot move plus a vol shift.

cards.hook: Turnover, not Sharpe, tells you how fragile your edge is.
cards.body: Say a signal earns 6 bps per round trip gross. Costs are 3 bps round trip. Net edge is half the gross, and **break-even cost multiple** (gross edge divided by round-trip cost) is 2x. That ratio, not Sharpe, tells you how much slippage error you can survive. Turnover multiplies the exposure: the same signal traded daily pays costs roughly 20 times as often as traded monthly. Options make it harsher because spreads are wide in percentage terms and widen in stress, when your signal fires hardest. Under 2x, assume live trading kills it.
cards.depth: Compute the multiple per strategy before you compare Sharpes. Then stress it: double the spread and add a 1 tick adverse fill on every order. If the strategy survives that, the edge is more likely real. If it only works at mid-price, you have a model of the quote screen, not of the market.

cards.hook: Until the 1990s, networks were barred from owning their own hits.
cards.body: The FCC's financial interest and syndication rules, adopted in 1970, restricted the big three networks from taking ownership stakes in the shows they aired and from domestic syndication. The aim was to break network control of programming. The result was a **separation of distribution from ownership** that fed a studio-driven production and syndication business. The rules were repealed in the 1990s, and within a few years networks and studios merged back together under common owners. Streaming rhymes with the pre-1970 world: the platform that distributes is again the entity that owns the show.
cards.depth: The practical effect for lawyers was the shape of every network deal: license fees below cost, with the studio deficit-financing and betting on the back end. When the rules fell, that bet changed. A vertically integrated owner can afford to lose on the first run because it keeps the whole life of the asset.

cards.hook: Write 'if X, then Y' in advance. It offloads inhibition.
cards.body: Implementation intentions, studied by Peter Gollwitzer since the 1990s, are plans in the form **if cue, then action**. The mechanism: the cue itself triggers the response more automatically, so you spend less effortful inhibition in the moment. That is the resource ADHD taxes. Reported effects in ADHD samples are smaller and less studied than in general populations, so treat this as a cheap test, not a cure. Pick your single top derailer and write one rule: if I sit at my desk, then my phone goes face-down in the drawer. Rehearse the sentence, not the intention.
cards.depth: Specificity is the whole trick. 'If I get distracted, I refocus' has no cue to attach to. A good cue is an observable event (sitting down, closing a call, hearing the dishwasher finish) and a good action takes under 10 seconds. Review after a week and replace any rule you never triggered.

cards.hook: An agent that passes once may fail every third run.
cards.body: Agent evals often report pass@k: did at least one of k tries succeed? That flatters you. What users feel is pass^k: did **all k runs succeed**. At a 90% per-run success rate, five consecutive successes happen only about 59% of the time (0.9 to the fifth power). A workflow that runs daily is a pass^k problem. So report per-run reliability alongside best-of-k, and pick the threshold from how often the task actually repeats. Reliability, not peak capability, usually decides whether you can leave an agent unattended.
cards.depth: The pass^k framing appears in tau-bench, which tests tool-using agents on repeated trials of the same task. Practical move: run each eval case 5 to 10 times, log the success rate per case, and sort by the flakiest. Those cases usually point at a missing instruction or an unverified tool result.

cards.hook: Halve the time left, and an ATM option loses only 29%.
cards.body: At-the-money option value scales roughly with the **square root of time**, not time itself. The Brenner-Subrahmanyam approximation puts an ATM price near 0.4 x spot x vol x sqrt(T). Cut T in half and sqrt(0.5) is about 0.71, so the option keeps roughly 71% of its value. Going from 60 days to 30 sheds about 29%, and 30 to 15 sheds another 29%. Dollar decay per day therefore accelerates as expiry nears, because it runs roughly as 1 over sqrt(T). Linear-decay intuition makes the first month of a short position look more generous than it is.
cards.depth: This is an ATM, low-rate, flat-vol approximation. Away from the money the decay profile differs, and skew shifts it further. Treat it as a mental model for sizing time exposure, not a pricing tool.

cards.hook: He sold cheap puts for years. One Monday erased everything.
cards.body: Victor Niederhoffer ran a celebrated fund and, reportedly, sold large quantities of deep out-of-the-money S&P 500 puts for premium. On October 27, 1997, Asian currency turmoil dragged the S&P down roughly 7% in one session. Puts that were nearly worthless became deeply in the money, margin calls hit, and his brokers liquidated positions into the panic. The market bounced hard within days, but the fund was already gone. **Being right eventually did not matter because he was liquidated first.** Short-tail strategies fail on the path, not the average.
cards.depth: The lesson is about funding and margin, not forecasting. A position you can't hold through the worst print isn't an edge, it's a countdown. Size to the liquidation path, not the expected value.

cards.hook: Experts anchor on the first number too, and deny it.
cards.body: In a classic 1987 study by Northcraft and Neale, real estate agents toured a house, then appraised it. Each saw a different listing price. Their appraisals tracked the listing price closely, yet the agents insisted they had ignored it. **Expertise did not protect them from the anchor.** So when the other side opens with a number, your private knowledge of the market won't shield you from it. Counter by putting your own principled number on the table before you respond to theirs, with a reason attached. Reacting to their figure is already negotiating on their ground.
cards.depth: Later anchoring research reported that deliberately focusing on the counterpart's target and alternatives, rather than their opening number, weakens the effect. Prepare that view before the call, not during it.

cards.hook: A subagent only knows what your brief tells it.
cards.body: A subagent starts with a blank context. It can't see your conversation, your files, or what you've already ruled out. That makes **the brief the entire interface**. A good one states the goal, what done looks like, what's already been tried, the boundaries, and the exact output format you want back. Anthropic reported that early versions of its multi-agent research system suffered from vague task descriptions, with agents duplicating each other's work or misreading the assignment. If two subagents could plausibly do the same thing from your brief, you have written it badly.
cards.depth: A cheap test: hand the brief to a smart contractor with no background. If they'd need to ask clarifying questions, the subagent will guess instead.

cards.hook: Recall it: which predicted kids' language-brain activity, words or turns?
cards.body: Think of the 2018 MIT scans of 4- to 6-year-olds. Hart and Risley's famous gap counted words heard. The brain data pointed elsewhere. **Back-and-forth conversational turns** predicted activity in Broca's area during language tasks, and verbal scores, independent of family income. Raw adult word count did not carry the effect. So the move is to say less and take more turns: ask something open, wait a beat, then build on what the child actually said.
cards.depth: It matters again because it changes the unit you track. Counting words rewards narrating at a child. Counting turns rewards listening, and a one-year-old's babble counts as a turn.

cards.hook: Expiring at your short strike means you might wake up with stock.
cards.body: A short put that closes right at the strike on expiration Friday is a coin flip you cannot see. Holders can submit exercise instructions until roughly 5:30 PM ET, well after the 4:00 PM close, so your assignment notice arrives after you can no longer trade out. If you are assigned, you own shares at Monday's open, with the gap risk that comes with them. This is **pin risk**. Close the position Friday afternoon, or trade cash-settled index options like XSP, where no shares ever change hands.
cards.depth: OCC auto-exercises equity options that finish $0.01 or more in the money, and holders can still exercise out-of-the-money contracts by instruction. A strike that closes at the money can flip either way, and weekend news lands on a position you can no longer hedge.

cards.hook: Your train and test folds leak across time. Purge them.
cards.body: Standard k-fold cross-validation assumes samples are independent. Financial labels are not. If each label looks five days ahead, a training row that ends the day before your test window shares most of its outcome with the first test row. The model memorizes the overlap and your out-of-sample score inflates.
