The fix, popularized by Marcos Lopez de Prado, is **purging**: drop any training row whose label window overlaps the test fold, then add an embargo, a short buffer after the test fold, to absorb serial correlation.
cards.depth: Purged k-fold is cheap to implement and almost always lowers your scores. Treat the drop from the naive version as information: it measures how much of your apparent edge was leakage rather than signal. If the edge vanishes, it was never there.

cards.hook: Eat before the pill kicks in. Appetite won't be there later.
cards.body: Appetite suppression is one of the most common stimulant side effects, and it tracks the drug's effect, typically strongest from mid-morning into the afternoon. The move is mechanical: eat a real, protein-heavy breakfast before the dose takes hold, then plan a calorie-dense meal for when it wears off. Skipping lunch and absorbing the whole day's deficit at 9 PM is **front-loading the deficit**, and it is predictable, so you can design around it. If intake stays low for weeks, raise it with your prescriber.
cards.depth: Amphetamine raises dopamine and norepinephrine signaling, which dampens hunger cues. Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug, so onset is gradual, roughly an hour or two, which gives you a real window to eat first.

cards.hook: Averaging forecasters works only if their errors differ.
cards.body: The diversity prediction theorem is an identity, not a hope: the crowd's squared error equals the average individual squared error minus the variance of the predictions. Ten forecasters who read the same sources make the same mistake, so the second term is near zero and averaging buys you nothing. **Diversity of error** is the asset. When you build a panel, whether of analysts, models, or friends, select for different information and methods, not just for the highest individual accuracy.
cards.depth: Tetlock's forecasting tournaments reported that aggregating independent forecasts beat most individual forecasters. Aggregation helps most when people hold genuinely different information, and least when they all anchor on the same headline.

cards.hook: Earn-outs price disagreement. They also manufacture it.
cards.body: An earn-out lets a buyer and seller who disagree about the future settle with a bet: pay more if the business hits a target. It works until the seller realizes the buyer now controls the levers. Cost allocation, integration choices, and pricing can all push the metric down, and sellers pay for that lack of control with litigation. Earn-out disputes are reported to be among the more commonly litigated M&A provisions. The same logic applies to any **revenue-based bonus**: whoever defines and controls the metric holds the power.
cards.depth: Practical protections: fix the metric's accounting policies at signing, add covenants on the specific levers that matter, include audit rights, and consider acceleration if the business is sold before the earn-out period ends.

cards.hook: Recall it: why does index vol trade below its components?
cards.body: Hint: it isn't averaging, and it isn't a pricing error. Index variance depends on how tightly the members move together. When correlation sits below one, idiosyncratic moves cancel inside the index, so **implied index vol runs below the average component vol**. The gap is implied correlation, and dispersion desks sell the richer index leg against the cheaper single names. That makes the book short correlation: it collects in calm, stock-picking markets and gets hurt when everything sells off together.
cards.depth: Whenever you hear 'dispersion', translate it to 'short correlation'. The losing scenario is the same one that hurts every short-vol book: correlation snaps toward one in a crash, and index vol reprices upward faster than the single names you own. Cheap insurance on the wrong leg.

cards.hook: Every peek at your holdout data spends it.
cards.body: A holdout set is only clean the first time you score it. Look at the result, adjust a filter, rerun, and the data has quietly become **training data that you labeled as test data**. Ten rounds of peeking is ten rounds of fitting, just done by hand instead of by optimizer. The discipline is procedural: decide the final candidate before touching the last slice, score it once, and accept whatever comes back, including a bad number.
cards.depth: Financial data adds a second leak: overlapping labels. If a trade's outcome spans several days, neighboring train and test rows share information. Purging and embargoing the rows near each split boundary, as in purged cross-validation, closes that leak, and it matters more the longer your holding period.

cards.hook: The first AI-training fair-use loss involved no chatbot.
cards.body: In February 2025, a Delaware federal court ruled in Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence that Ross's use of Westlaw headnotes to train a legal search tool was not fair use. The tool was **non-generative**: it returned existing case links, not new text. The court leaned on market substitution, since Ross aimed to compete with Westlaw. Later 2025 rulings involving generative models reached different conclusions on training, so the line practitioners now argue over is what the output does to the original's market.
cards.depth: The decision went up on interlocutory appeal to the Third Circuit, so check its current status before citing it. Its practical value for deal work: a training-data warranty should be analyzed by what the model does with the data, not by the label 'AI'.

cards.hook: Future rewards shrink faster for you. Pull one forward.
cards.body: Delay discounting is how steeply a reward loses value as it gets further away, and research reports steeper discounting on average in ADHD. A deadline three weeks out is worth almost nothing to the part of the brain that decides what to do now. The move is not more willpower. **Attach something small and immediate to the first step**: the good coffee only while drafting, the podcast only during the filing. Then cut the far deadline into milestones due today or tomorrow.
cards.depth: This is temptation bundling plus deadline shortening. The test is behavioral: if the reward is available without doing the task, it is not bundled and it will not work. Keep the bundle exclusive, or it decays like every other system.

cards.hook: Don't buy information that can't change your decision.
cards.body: The value of information is the expected improvement in your decision, not how much you learn. If you would take the same action whatever the answer turns out to be, the information is worth **exactly zero**, however interesting or reassuring it feels. Before commissioning another report, comp analysis, or backtest, ask: which result would flip my choice, and how likely is that? If you cannot name one, you are paying for comfort.
cards.depth: The flip side is also useful. Information is most valuable when you are near the decision threshold, close to indifferent, and the stakes are large. Spend your diligence there, and stop spending it where the answer is already lopsided.

cards.hook: Your short strike's gamma explodes in the last week.
cards.body: Gamma on an at-the-money option scales roughly with the inverse of the square root of time left. A 30-day option has a modest gamma. The same strike with 3 days left can carry gamma several times larger. That means **delta swings hardest when you have the least time to adjust**. A 1% index move in the final days can flip a comfortable short strike into a position that gains or loses delta fast. Theta is richest here too, which is exactly why the trade feels safe right up until it isn't.
cards.depth: This is why many premium sellers close at 50% of max profit or around 21 days to expiration. They give up the last slice of theta to avoid the steepest part of the gamma curve. The tradeoff is real: you pay more commissions and slippage, but you cut exposure to a single bad week.

cards.hook: Your best parameter sits on a cliff edge.
cards.body: When you optimize a parameter, the winner is often a sharp peak surrounded by much worse results. That peak is usually noise you fitted. Prefer a **broad plateau**, where neighboring values perform similarly. If a 14-day lookback shines but 13 and 15 collapse, the edge is probably not there. A robust strategy degrades gracefully when you nudge its settings. A fragile one falls apart, and live markets will nudge it for you.
cards.depth: A practical check: plot performance across the full parameter grid as a heatmap and pick the center of the largest stable region, not the single best cell. Then confirm it on data the optimizer never touched.

cards.hook: Your AI-training license may not cover the model's outputs.
cards.body: Many data licenses grant rights to train on a work, but say nothing clear about what the resulting model can generate. That gap matters. A grant to "use for machine learning" is not obviously a grant to **commercialize outputs that resemble the source**. Practitioners keep drafting training clauses and leaving output rights, retention, and deletion on model weights undefined. If the licensor later terminates, nobody can say whether the weights must be retrained or destroyed.
cards.depth: Fix it in drafting: separate training rights, output rights, and post-termination obligations, and say expressly whether trained weights survive termination. Silence will be litigated, and courts have not settled how.

cards.hook: You keep a loser because selling makes it real.
cards.body: The disposition effect is the documented tendency to sell winners too early and hold losers too long. Realizing a loss feels like admitting error, so people wait for a recovery that the market owes them nothing. The fix is to ask a cleaner question: **would I buy this position today at this price**, with fresh cash and no history? If the answer is no, the only thing holding you in is the sunk cost, and sunk costs carry no information about the future.
cards.depth: Note the tax wrinkle: harvesting a loss can be worth real money, so the biased behavior is also the expensive one. Pre-committing exit rules before entry removes the in-the-moment emotion entirely.

cards.hook: Set the alarm for leaving, not for starting.
cards.body: Time blindness makes the transition cost invisible, so people plan to start a task at the last moment and run late. The move is to anchor an alert to the **departure time, minus the real travel and prep buffer**, not to the event itself. Then add a second alert at the buffer's midpoint. The first answers when to stop what you are doing. The second catches the drift that eats the gap. You are externalizing the one calculation your internal clock does not run.
cards.depth: Test it on one recurring commitment this week, such as daycare pickup, and log how often you leave on time with and without the earlier alert. A concrete comparison beats trusting the feeling.

cards.hook: Monthly SPX options settle at a price nobody ever traded.
cards.body: Standard third-Friday SPX options are AM-settled. Trading in them stops at Thursday's close, and settlement uses the **Special Opening Quotation**, which is built from each component stock's first trade on Friday morning. Those opens print at different moments, so the SOQ is a composite that may never show up as a live index level. For a short condor, that means an overnight gap you cannot adjust, close, or hedge with the option itself. A Thursday close comfortably inside your strikes guarantees nothing. SPXW weeklies and XSP are PM-settled at Friday's close, so the risk window stays tradable.
cards.depth: The SOQ is published under the ticker SET. On volatile mornings it can land well away from both Thursday's close and Friday's first printed index level, because stocks that open late are priced at their own first trade. Practical rule: if you carry a monthly SPX position into expiration, size it as if Friday's open could gap through you, or roll to the PM-settled weekly that expires the same day.

cards.hook: Your short-premium backtest shows Sharpe 2. Sharpe can't see the tail.
cards.body: Sharpe uses only two numbers, mean and standard deviation. A put-selling strategy earns small steady gains and loses rarely but big, so its returns are **negatively skewed with fat tails**. In any sample that happens to miss the crash, the standard deviation looks tame and the ratio looks elite. A better Sharpe estimate from the same data won't fix that. Ask how many tail events your history actually contains that the strategy is exposed to, and judge the ratio by that count, not by the decimal.
cards.depth: Bailey and Lopez de Prado's Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (2012) formalizes this: it discounts an observed Sharpe for negative skew, excess kurtosis, and a short track record, and gives the probability that the true Sharpe beats a benchmark. Run it on a few years of short-vol results and a headline 2.0 often stops looking convincing. Then stress-test by replaying paths like August 2015 and February 2018.

cards.hook: Stop mid-task on purpose. Tomorrow's start is already done.
cards.body: The expensive moment is restarting, not working. Starting cold means rebuilding the whole context in working memory before the first action is even visible, and that rebuild cost lands right on top of your activation threshold. So end every session **mid-step, with the next physical action written down**: 'paste clause 7 into the redline,' not 'finish the markup.' Leave the file open to that exact spot. Hemingway did a version of this, stopping when he still knew what would happen next. You're doing the hardest part of tomorrow's start while the context is still loaded.
cards.depth: Why it works: much of what makes starting hard is the planning that a vague first step demands, and planning is executive work, the exact function under strain. A written next action moves that plan out of your head and onto the page. Pair it with a visible cue, like the open file or a note on the keyboard, so picking it back up doesn't depend on remembering to look.

cards.hook: Every scene ends worse. Every sequel ends with a decision.
cards.body: Dwight Swain's Techniques of the Selling Writer (1965) splits fiction into two alternating units, **scene and sequel**. A scene is goal, conflict, disaster: the character wants something now, meets opposition, and leaves worse off or holding a new problem. A sequel is reaction, dilemma, decision: they feel the blow, weigh bad options, and choose, which sets the next goal. Alternating them gives you momentum with room to breathe. To diagnose a dead stretch, ask which unit it is and which beat is missing. Usually it's a scene with no disaster, so nothing changed.
cards.depth: For a sleep story, invert it on purpose. Build mostly from sequel-shaped material, like small reactions and gentle choices, and swap each disaster for a resolution, so every beat lowers tension instead of raising it. Knowing how the machine works is what lets you switch tension off deliberately rather than by accident.

cards.hook: Count conversational turns, not words. The brain did.
cards.body: Hart and Risley's famous '30 million word gap' counted words heard, and later work has contested both the size of the gap and the method. A 2018 MIT study led by Rachel Romeo scanned 4- to 6-year-olds and found that **back-and-forth conversational turns**, not the raw number of adult words, predicted activity in Broca's area during language tasks and predicted verbal scores, independent of family income. The practical move costs nothing: say less, ask something open, wait an extra beat, then build on what the child actually said. Narrating at a toddler is input. Taking turns is the workout.
cards.depth: Caveat: it's a correlational study of 36 children, so it shows an association, not proof that turns cause the growth. But it fits the wider serve-and-return research championed by Harvard's Center on the Developing Child, and the habit has essentially no downside. The extra wait for an answer is the part most adults skip.

cards.hook: Exercising a call early makes sense only before a dividend.
cards.body: An American call is almost never worth exercising before expiry. Exercise and you throw away the option's remaining time value and give up the interest on cash you haven't spent yet. **The lone exception is the day before an ex-dividend date.** If the dividend you'd collect by owning the shares outright exceeds the call's remaining time value, capturing it beats holding the option. That is the only time rational early exercise of a call appears, and it clusters entirely around dividend dates. Miss the ex-date and the reason evaporates.
cards.depth: Puts are the mirror. A deep in-the-money put can be worth exercising early for the interest on the proceeds, any time, no dividend needed. Calls need the dividend, puts need the rates. Same parity, opposite triggers.

cards.hook: You overweight tiny probabilities. That is why lottery tickets sell.
cards.body: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory found people don't use probabilities straight. They run them through a weighting function: a 1% chance feels more like 5%, and a 99% chance feels more like 90%. **Small probabilities get overweighted, large ones underweighted.** Overweighting the tail is why the same person buys both a lottery ticket and flood insurance. Underweighting near-certainty is why people pay a premium to erase the final sliver of risk. In options it shows up as far-out-of-the-money contracts trading persistently rich: buyers are paying for a lottery, not an expected value.
cards.depth: The trade looks obvious and is dangerous: sell what others overpay for. But the overweighting isn't pure error. Tails are fatter than the normal curve claims, and the one time the lottery hits, the seller pays back years of collected premium at once.

cards.hook: Your best system quietly stops working once it stops being new.
cards.body: An ADHD brain under-responds to cues that aren't novel or salient. That is why a new app, a fresh checklist, or a relocated sticky note works for two weeks and then quietly stops. It didn't fail. **It habituated into the background, and an invisible cue cues nothing.** This is tool decay, and it is predictable, not a character flaw. The move: engineer novelty on purpose. Rotate the tool's form, color, or location on a schedule, or swap it before it goes invisible. Treat any single system as a consumable with a short shelf life, not a permanent fix you failed to maintain.
cards.depth: Why novelty works: dopamine signaling tracks prediction error, the gap between expected and actual. A novel cue carries prediction error and grabs attention; a fully predicted one carries none. Rotating the system keeps manufacturing small prediction errors, which is what keeps it salient enough to act on.

cards.hook: California voids a vague AI-likeness clause even if you signed it.
cards.body: California's AB 2602 took effect January 1, 2025. It makes a contract term allowing a digital replica of someone's voice or likeness, used in place of work they'd otherwise do in person, unenforceable when two things are both true: the clause lacks a reasonably specific description of the intended uses, and the person wasn't represented by a lawyer or a union negotiating for them. **A broad catch-all replica grant, signed, can simply be void.** The old instinct to draft the widest possible rights grant now cuts against you here. For an unrepresented individual, vagueness is no longer leverage, it's a hole in your own contract.
cards.depth: The representation prong is the quiet part. If a union or counsel negotiated the clause, the specificity requirement relaxes. The statute is aimed at the unrepresented individual signing a studio's boilerplate, not at a repped client with a lawyer across the table.

cards.hook: Recall it: what actually destroyed XIV on Volmageddon day?
cards.body: February 5, 2018. The VIX nearly doubled, but that alone wouldn't have killed the product. Before you read on, try to name the mechanical trigger. The answer: inverse-volatility notes like XIV had to rebalance daily, so the spike forced them to **buy VIX futures into the close, in size the market couldn't absorb.** That buying pushed futures higher, which forced still more buying, a loop that fed itself. XIV lost roughly 96% and was terminated within days.
cards.depth: The reusable lesson isn't that volatility is dangerous. It's that any product with forced, size-insensitive daily rebalancing becomes its own worst counterparty in a crisis. Before you hold or sell one, ask what it is mechanically required to buy at the worst possible moment.

cards.hook: Puts cost more than equally far-out calls. Always.
cards.body: Equity index options carry a persistent skew: out-of-the-money puts trade at higher implied vol than out-of-the-money calls the same distance away. Two forces drive it. Crash risk is one-sided, so hedgers and funds constantly bid up downside protection. And volatility rises when markets fall, so a lower strike genuinely deserves a higher vol. The result is **the volatility smirk**, and it means your short put is selling expensive insurance while your short call is selling cheap. Skew is not a glitch. It is the market pricing fear asymmetrically.
cards.depth: The second force is the leverage effect: as a stock falls, its debt-to-equity ratio rises, making the equity riskier and more volatile, so lower strikes earn higher vol honestly. Buyers of crash protection also pay a variance risk premium on top. That is why selling downside skew pays on average, and why it hurts most exactly when everyone needs the hedge at once.

cards.hook: A positive expected value can still ruin you.
cards.body: Flip a coin each round. Heads, your stake grows 50 percent. Tails, it shrinks 40 percent. The expected value per round is plus 5 percent, so the naive read says bet everything, forever. Do it and you go broke with near certainty. The average across many parallel gamblers rises, but **almost every individual path trends to zero**, because gains and losses compound multiplicatively, not additively. The number that actually governs your fate is the geometric mean, about 0.95 per round, a 5 percent loss every time. Expected value answered the wrong question.
cards.depth: This is the ergodicity problem. The ensemble average (many people, one round) and the time average (one person, many rounds) diverge whenever outcomes multiply. Trading is multiplicative. It is also the deep reason Kelly sizing exists: bet to maximize the geometric growth rate, not the arithmetic expectation, or the math that looks like edge quietly bankrupts you over time.

cards.hook: A court made OpenAI keep chats users had deleted.
cards.body: In the New York Times copyright suit, a federal magistrate ordered OpenAI to preserve and segregate ChatGPT output logs it would normally delete, including conversations users had chosen to erase. The Times wanted the trove to hunt for regurgitation of its articles. The order collided head-on with OpenAI's own deletion promises and with privacy regimes like the GDPR. **A litigation hold beat the delete button.** For anyone building a product on generative models, the lesson is blunt: your retention policy is only as real as the next discovery request that overrides it.
cards.depth: Preservation duties attach once litigation is reasonably anticipated, and they reach data the business would otherwise purge. Synthetic-output products make that scope enormous, because every prompt and completion becomes potentially discoverable evidence. Practitioners are now drafting around it: narrower logging by default, clearer legal-hold carve-outs in privacy notices, and segregation plans built before the first subpoena lands, not after.

cards.hook: ADHD doesn't ignore bedtime. Its body clock runs late.
cards.body: A large share of ADHD adults carry a delayed circadian rhythm: the brain releases melatonin one to two hours later than typical, so 'go to bed earlier' fails because the biology is not ready for sleep yet. Willpower at 11 PM cannot move a clock that light sets. The lever that actually shifts it is **bright light within an hour of waking**, which advances the whole cycle earlier over several days. Ten to fifteen minutes of real outdoor light in the morning does more than any amount of forcing the pillow at night.
cards.depth: Melatonin onset, not bedtime, anchors the rhythm. Evening screens push it later; morning light pulls it forward through the retinal pathway to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. The concrete move: light first, then caffeine and a hard first task. And hold the wake time fixed even on weekends, because a drifting wake time lets the late clock quietly reset later all over again.

cards.hook: Try enough strategies and one looks brilliant by pure luck.
cards.body: Overfitting is not only about tuning parameters. It hides in the count of strategies you tried before keeping the winner. Test a hundred random rules on the same data and, by chance alone, a few will post gorgeous Sharpe ratios. Report only the survivor and you have fooled yourself completely. The fix is to **penalize the Sharpe for the number of trials**, the way the deflated Sharpe ratio does. A 2.0 Sharpe from one honest test and a 2.0 cherry-picked from five hundred are not the same discovery.
cards.depth: Under the null of no skill, the expected maximum Sharpe across many trials rises with both the number of trials and the backtest length. Bailey and Lopez de Prado's deflated Sharpe adjusts for exactly that, plus the return series' skew and fat tails. If you cannot state how many configurations you ran, your best result is uninterpretable. Track the trial count like a cost.
